doc.title: Victor Rendon interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 12, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Black Lives Matter and the Chicano Movement
summary: He recalls becoming aware of the Chicano Movement in Texas around 1970-71 and links Mexican-American injustice to today's protests.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: But it’s an honest answer. The one crisis on top of another, in the midst of all this now we have a social crisis with the Black Lives Matter gatherings, some protests, and I’m going to go out on a limb here and I wonder if the Latino community, being classified as a minority, if their thinking is different about this current situation, rather than the white/Caucasian majority.

Well you know I was a little young during the 60s, I was only in my early teens back in the 60s when we had the Civil Rights Movement. But later, like around 70, 71, that’s when I became somewhat aware of what we call the Chicano Movement in Texas. That was the same type of thing as demanding equal rights for, in particular, Mexican Americans. Because you know of course the blacks, African-Americans have been discriminated with the restraints and all that stuff. The Mexican-Americans also suffered injustices in the Southwest you know? For one thing the whole Southwest was taken from © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

Mexico, you know that’s a whole history in itself. So we do have a history of you know, discrimination, injustice. So I feel that it is important. When I hear about injustices to African-Americans I feel that it reflects what we need for us also, and for everybody, you know, all minorities. So yes, I do feel that it’s important. And it goes, it covers everybody and any type of situation.
